summary: Kole Jain codes three website load animations with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the GSAP library, as part 2 of a series that first designed them as Figma prototypes. The first is a loading screen: a black full-screen overlay where the logo fades in, then the overlay slides up while the hero text slides up from below and the navbar fades in last. The second is a navbar that grows from a dot into a circle, stretches into a pill, and then fades its items in one after another. The third is a text wipe, where a colored block (its background color copied from elsewhere in the stylesheet) sweeps across a headline and retracts to reveal it. For the big moves he uses the expo.inOut ease to match the custom curves from the Figma prototypes, and builds each animation as a paused timeline of chained steps. For a design system, it shows how a designed motion curve and a few timing values carry over into code, and how to order steps so related moves run together or in sequence.
key_ideas: A load animation can be built as a GSAP timeline: a chain of steps that run one after another unless told to overlap.
The expo.inOut ease reproduces the look and feel of the custom bezier curves designed in the Figma prototype.
Elements that animate in are first put in their starting state (opacity 0, width 0%, max-width 0px, or a yPercent offset), set either in CSS or with gsap.set.
Related moves can run together: the hero text slides up at the same moment the loading screen slides away, using the "<" position marker.
Moving an element by yPercent uses a percentage of the element's own height, not the viewport's.
A pill navbar can grow from a dot: scale from 0 to 1, then widen max-width from the bar's own height (a circle) to its full width.
Reading an element's real height with gsap.getProperty lets the animation start as a perfect circle.
Stagger fades a group of items in one at a time with a single call, instead of one call per item.
A text wipe grows a colored block across the text, makes the text visible underneath, then anchors the block to the right and shrinks it away.
The navbar simply fades in at the end over 0.3; the source says it doesn't need an ease per se.
You might need to play with the timings a little after the first run.

rules.rule: Use the expo.inOut ease for the large load-animation moves (the loading screen sliding away, the navbar widening, the text wipe) so the code matches the custom bezier curves designed in Figma.
rules.why: It gives the same look and feel as the custom beziers in the Figma prototype.
rules.evidence: set our ease to Expo in out and this is important

rules.rule: Put each element that will animate in into its hidden starting state (opacity 0, width 0% or max-width 0px), in CSS or with gsap.set, before the timeline runs.
rules.why: The element disappears first so it can be animated in with JavaScript.
rules.evidence: this opacity to zero okay and so that's going to make our element here disappear

rules.rule: When a loading screen slides away, slide the content beneath it up at the same time by starting its step with the "<" position marker instead of chaining it after.
rules.why: The things underneath should also slide up, and a chained step would otherwise start only after the previous one ends.
rules.evidence: we can then animate it up up while our loading screen is moving up

rules.rule: Offset text below its resting place with yPercent so the distance is relative to the element's own height, then animate it back to 0.
rules.why: yPercent 100 is 100% of the element's length, not 100% of the viewport.
rules.evidence: it's 100% of the length of this element

rules.rule: Fade the navbar in last, after the loading screen and hero text have slid up, with a short fade and no special ease.
rules.why: The navbar should appear after everything has slid up; the source says it doesn't need an ease.
rules.evidence: we want our navbar to fade in after everything has slid up

rules.rule: Build a loading screen as a fixed overlay at top 0 and left 0, 100vw by 100vh, with a high z-index, a black background and flex centering for the logo.
rules.why: Top and left 0 avoid spacing issues, the z-index keeps it on top of everything, and flex centers the logo container.

rules.rule: To make a pill navbar grow from a dot, first scale it from 0 to 1, then animate max-width from the bar's measured height up to its full width with expo.inOut.
rules.why: Starting max-width at the bar's height makes width equal height, so the bar starts as a circle before stretching.
rules.evidence: max width okay so make sure to remember

rules.rule: Measure the navbar's rendered height with gsap.getProperty and use it as the starting max-width.
rules.why: The width must equal the height to get a circle, and getProperty returns the real height (27 pixels here).

rules.rule: Set the navbar's CSS max-width to 0px before animating max-width with fromTo.
rules.why: If you don't change it, the animation isn't going to work very well.
rules.evidence: make sure to remember to come back here

rules.rule: Fade a group of navbar items in one after another with a single staggered call on an array of the items.
rules.why: It is faster and easier than selecting and animating each item one at a time.

rules.rule: For a text wipe, grow a colored block from 0% to 100% width over the text, make the text visible, anchor the block to the right, then shrink it back to 0%.
rules.why: The wipe starts on the left and finishes on the right, revealing the text behind it.
rules.evidence: width of that to 100% um we'll set the duration to be equal to 1

rules.rule: If right: 0 alone does not move the wipe block's anchor to the right, also set left to auto.
rules.why: Setting right to 0 is often all you need, but sometimes left also has to be auto for it to work.
rules.evidence: set left to Auto in order for it to work

rules.rule: If the full-size wipe block looks too large, shrink its height (80% here) and move it down (top 10%) so the bottom of the text is still covered.
rules.why: At full size the block was larger than wanted, and after shrinking it the bottom of the text showed until it was moved down.

rules.rule: Style the navbar as a translucent pill: an outer section that centers the nav container, which uses flex with space-between and centered items, a background color with alpha 61, border-radius 100px, and padding of 10px on top and 30px on the sides.
rules.why: The source adds these so the bar looks better before animating it.
rules.evidence: add a border radius as well we'll do 100 pixels

rules.rule: On the loading screen, wrap the logo image and the brand name in one container set to display flex with a small gap (10px) and centered content, so they sit side by side in the middle and fade in as one.
rules.why: The container lets the logo be centered, and the logo should sit right beside the text rather than one on top of the other.
rules.evidence: so that we can Center it later

rules.rule: Give the navbar width: 100% alongside max-width: 500px, because max-width on its own does not size the bar.
rules.why: The source notes that max-width alone is not actually going to do anything, so a width has to be set as well.
rules.evidence: that's not actually going to do anything

decisions.question: Which load animation should greet visitors when the site opens?

options.name: Loading screen
options.effect: A black full-screen overlay shows the logo and name fading in, then slides up to reveal the page while the hero text slides up with it.
options.when: When you want a branded moment before the hero appears [inferred].

options.name: Expanding navbar
options.effect: The navbar grows from a tiny dot into a circle, stretches into a pill, then its items fade in one by one.
options.when: When the navbar is the element to draw attention to on landing [inferred].

options.name: Text wipe
options.effect: A colored block sweeps across a large headline and retracts to the right, revealing the text.
options.when: When a big headline carries the page [inferred].

decisions.evidence: a loading screen animation an expanding navbar and a text wipe effect

decisions.question: Should the next step of the load animation wait for the previous one or run at the same time?

options.name: One after another (default)
options.effect: Each step starts right after the previous one ends, like the logo fade, then the screen slide, then the navbar fade.
options.when: When one move should finish before the next starts, such as fading the navbar in after everything has slid up.

options.name: At the same time ("<")
options.effect: The step starts with the one before it, so the hero text rises together with the loading screen.
options.when: When the content underneath should move along with the element leaving.

decisions.recommendation: Run the hero text slide-up at the same time as the loading screen slide-up, and fade the navbar in afterwards.
decisions.evidence: normally it would start right after but we want them to happen concurrently

decisions.question: Where should an element's hidden starting state be set: in CSS or in JavaScript with gsap.set?

options.name: CSS
options.effect: The element is hidden by the stylesheet (for example opacity 0) before any script runs.
options.when: Used here for the logo container and the text wipe's width.

options.name: gsap.set
options.effect: The script hides or offsets the element (for example the navbar's opacity or the header text's yPercent) before the timeline runs.
options.when: Used here for the navbar and the header text on the loading-screen page.

decisions.evidence: you can also do it in CSS there are pros and cons

decisions.question: How should several navbar items be faded in?

options.name: One call per item
options.effect: Each item is selected and faded separately.
options.when: The source calls it totally a viable option.

options.name: One staggered call
options.effect: All items go in an array and fade in one after another from a single call (stagger 0.2, duration 0.6).
options.when: When you want it faster and easier to write.

decisions.recommendation: A single staggered call, because it is faster and easier.
decisions.evidence: might be a little faster and easier to do

decisions.question: Should an animation step state only where it ends (to) or both where it starts and ends (fromTo)?

options.name: to
options.effect: Only the end position is set, for example opacity 1 after the CSS already set opacity 0.
options.when: Used here for the logo fade, the loading-screen slide and the text wipe.

options.name: fromTo
options.effect: Both a start and an end position are set, for example scale 0 to 1, or max-width from the bar's height to 500px.
options.when: Used here for the navbar, which starts as a dot and then a circle.

decisions.evidence: use a from two instead of just a two

process.detail: Design the load animations in Figma with custom bezier curves (part 1 of the series), then develop them in code.
Set up the page's HTML and CSS without motion, such as a navbar and a hero with a background image and absolutely positioned text.
Add the extra element the animation needs: the loading-screen section, the nav container or the text-wipe block, and style it in CSS.
Set what will animate in to its hidden start: opacity 0, width 0%, max-width 0px, or a yPercent offset with gsap.set.
Create a gsap.timeline with paused set to true.
Add steps with to, fromTo and set, giving each a duration, an ease (expo.inOut for the big moves) and an optional delay; use "<" for steps that should run together and stagger for groups.
Call play() on the timeline, with the brackets.
Reload the page to watch the result and adjust the timings as needed.

caveats: Auto-generated captions: GSAP is heard as "gap", expo.inOut as "Expo in out", yPercent as "y%", getProperty as "getet property", to and fromTo as "two" and "from two", navbar as "Navar" and z-index as "Zed index"; the "<" position marker is described only as typing quotes and "this back arrow", and the variable "LMS" is read as elms [inferred]. Numbers were not changed.
This is a code-along tutorial: the values (500px, 1-second delay, 0.2 stagger) fit this demo page, and the source says you might need to play with the timings.
The custom bezier curves from the Figma prototype are in part 1 of the series; this video gives no curve values, only the expo.inOut ease that approximates them.
The duration of the first logo fade-in is not stated.
The first timeline (the loading screen) is created paused, but the transcript never shows play() being called on it; play() is only shown for the navbar and the text wipe.
The caption text around the end of the navbar section is garbled, so the finished navbar result is not described in words.
Published March 2024; the GSAP calls shown are from that time [inferred].
The video does not discuss reduced-motion settings or how long a loading screen holds back the content [inferred].
